## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Aṭṭhānajātaka* (Ja 425) is a narrative in the Jātaka collection whose title translates as "Impossible" [SuttaCentral]. In the commentary's narrative frame, the story opens with the verse line *gaṅgākumudinī* and is delivered by the Buddha while residing at Jetavana [Fausböll 1883]. It is prompted by a backsliding monk overcome by sensual passion; the Buddha rebukes him by pointing out that womankind are ungrateful, treacherous, and impossible to satisfy, recalling how in the past even a thousand coins a day could not earn a woman's enduring loyalty [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. The core tale, which illustrates these points alongside a catalogue of natural impossibilities, recounts the enduring friendship established during their education between the prince of Benares and the son of the city's *seṭṭhi* [Dutt 1956; von Glasenapp 1966]. At the conclusion of the sermon, the backsliding monk attains stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), and the Buddha identifies the former king as Ānanda and the ascetic sage as himself [Fausböll 1883].
According to SuttaCentral, no curated canonical parallels are recorded for Ja 425, though modern translations exist in four languages [SuttaCentral]. Computational analysis via DharmaNexus indicates substantial Pali-internal text reuse with the third volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (over 1,800 characters across four segments) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also detects cross-language textual alignments with several Mahāyāna scriptures, chiefly the Sanskrit *Suvarṇaprabhāsasūtra* and its Tibetan versions, as well as the Tibetan *Mahāmeghasūtra* [DharmaNexus].
